newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss cabinet taps members for Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss cabinet taps members for Holocaust fund.

text.p: The Swiss government named the country's top Jewish leader on Wednesday as chairman of a humanitarian fund for Holocaust survivors created under international pressure over Switzerland's World War Two role.

The Federal Council, or cabinet, said in a statement Rolf Bloch, president of the Swiss Jewish Federation, would head the board of seven directors who will administer 265 million Swiss francs pledged by banks and companies.
It also appointed three other Swiss members of the board and urged world Jewish groups, who are suposed to have a major say in distributing the money, to present their candidates quickly.
Bloch had already been tipped as a probable chairman in order to strike a 50-50 balance between Jewish representatives and Swiss citizens.
The government approved the memorial fund in February but its launch, initially set for March 1, has been delayed as Berne and world Jewish groups moved more slowly than expected on nominations.

The agreement by both sides was for the government to appoint four members including the president while three would be named by the World Jewish Restitution Organisation (WJRO), an umbrella group of major Jewish organisations and the state of Israel.
"In order for the fund to begin its work as quickly as possible, the Federal Council urged the WJRO to present its nominations soon," the cabinet statement said.
Sources close to the fund had earlier told Reuters they expected Nobel Peace Prize winner Eli Wiesel, a survivor of two concentration camps, to be named chairman.

They said Romanian-born Wiesel, who received the 1986 Nobel peace prize for his work in exposing the horrors of the Holocaust, had initially been reluctant to accept the post but agreed out of a sense of obligation.

Berne's creation of the fund in February helped to defuse the country's worst foreign policy crisis since World War Two, sparked by allegations that Swiss banks hoarded unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims and that neutral Switzerland cynically profited from the war.
Galvanised by international pressure and boycott threats, the three biggest Swiss banks launched the fund with a 100 million franc donation.
The Swiss National Bank has also promised 100 million francs and smaller banks and other businesses have donated 65 million.
Officials have said a large part of the money is likely to go to Jewish groups and individuals in Eastern Europe who were cut off from compensation for decades by the Iron Curtain.

The fund is separate from a proposed seven billion Swiss franc Solidarity Foundation that would sell official gold reserves to finance aid to victims of poverty, catastrophes and human rights outrages, including the Holocaust.
